newsitem.title: USA: How consumers would fare if CEOs ruled the U.S..
newsitem.headline: How consumers would fare if CEOs ruled the U.S..

text.p: If chief executive officers of the nation's largest corporations ran the country, consumers might not have to pay a lot of taxes but runaway inflation or a recession could be in the offing.
The nation's business leaders believe a balanced budget, greater access to global markets and lower capital gains taxes are keys to a healthy U.S. economy, according to a new survey.

The CEOs indicated that if the economy improves, consumers will benefit as well. But the authors of the survey conducted by the Bureau of Business Research at American International College in Springfield, Mass., believe the implications for consumers may not be so rosy if CEOs have their way, regardless of what the president and Congress do.

Most of the CEOs (87 percent) said lower capital gains taxes for businesses and individuals would help long-term growth in the nation's Gross Domestic Product, the main barometer of U.S. economic health, while keeping inflation under 3 percent.

However, said finance professor Ira Smolowitz, a co-author of the survey, the executives are "keen on lower capital gains taxes, but the evidence is not clear whether this stimulates private savings."
Adequate amounts of savings on a consumer level are needed so the economy can keep moving, he said. People are more likely to spend if there is something in the bank, thus stimulating the economy.
However, a cut in capital gains taxes may not have the desired effect of inducing people to add to their savings, the survey's authors believe.
Almost two-thirds of the executives (65.8 percent) favored a balanced budget amendment that would require the U.S. government to pare down the deficit to zero over several years.
President Clinton said recently his budget office expects the fiscal 1997 budget defict to be around $37 billion, down from $107 billion in fiscal 1996.
"A balanced budget amendment means that the government has to live within its means, it can't borrow much, and can't mitigate against the business cycle of ups and downs," Smolowitz said.

During an economic downturn, for example, the government may want to stimulate the economy by spending more than it takes in. During good times, it would be unlikely for the government to reduce its budget voluntarily, he said.

By not being able to borrow, this could "trigger runaway inflation or recession. You want the government to spend more to stimulate the economy (during a recession), since it is not coming from the private sector," Smolowitz said.

Executives said overwhelmingly (92 percent) that the government's efforts for greater free trade would aid the economy, but only half felt efforts to restrict trade or punish unfair trading partners would help the country.
This suggests that U.S. firms are willing to accept an uneven playing field as long as there is access to new markets.

"A key to long-term health of the U.S. economy is to invest profits in long-term strategies to increase corporate long-term competitiveness. This is not an inducement for many U.S. firms, given the lure of huge profits and short-term pressure from stockholders and competition in an ever-changing marketplace," said Clayton Hillyer, study co-author and marketing professor at AIC.
Only 47 percent of the CEOs said tax deductions for higher education would have a positive impact on the U.S. economy.
Smolowitz, as an academic, took a dim view of the executives' "cynical view on tuition credit.
"This is an information-based society and colleges have an increasing role in society," he said.

Regarding a flat personal income tax, such as that proposed by Steve Forbes, a 1996 Presidential candidate, 57.9 percent of the CEOs said it would have a positive impact, 26.3 percent said it would have a negative impact, and 15.8 percent said it would have no impact.
The study's authors explained that some executives believe a simplification of the tax code will lead to increased compliance and eliminate loopholes.
One surprising result was that only 16 percent favored limiting the discretion of Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan to guide money supply, interest rates and other fiscal policies.
Smolowitz said people favor a human pilot over an autopilot, "despite an occasionally bumpy ride."

The survey involved chief executive officers from 39 firms on the Forbes 500 list in banking, insurance, retail, transportation, manufacturing, computers, telecommunications, publishing, energy and consumer products.
The survey was completed in late July.
